scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Let me break this down step by step. First, the situation: schools are closed, so the student and her younger sister are at home. Their dad works from home, but their mom still goes to her office. The mom expects them to cook dinner every night because they're home all day. The student is annoyed because even though they're home, they have schoolwork to do. When she confronts her mom about it, things escalate, and the mom gets upset, calling them useless and expressing shame. The student is also pointing out that her mom is a terrible cook and doesn't put any effort into improving her skills. The dad, on the other hand, is an excellent cook and often ends up making dinner, even when he's exhausted from work. The student herself is a good cook and has been helping out, but with schoolwork piling up, she's struggling to keep up with the cooking demands. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong for the student to refuse to cook dinner and tell her mom not to expect it every night? Let me think about this from different angles. 1. **Responsibility and Expectations:** - The mom expects the kids to cook because they're home. Is that a fair expectation? On one hand, the kids are at home, so it might seem reasonable for the mom to expect some help. On the other hand, the kids are still students with schoolwork, which is their priority. It's a balance between contributing to the household and managing academic responsibilities. 2. **Workload and Fairness:** - The mom is at work, but she still expects the kids to handle cooking. Meanwhile, the dad is handling most of the chores and cooking when he gets home. It seems like the mom isn't pulling her weight, which is frustrating for the family. The student is pointing out that the mom doesn't contribute much, which adds to the unfairness. 3. **Emotional Impact:** - The mom's reaction to not having dinner ready was harsh, calling the kids useless and expressing shame. That's emotionally damaging and unfair. The student was already stressed about schoolwork and then had to deal with her mom's anger, which isn't constructive. 4. **Personal Boundaries:** - The student is asserting her boundaries by refusing to cook every night. It's important for her to set limits, especially when her mental and academic health are at stake. However, how she communicates this is crucial. Being confrontational might escalate tensions, but standing up for herself is valid. 5. **Alternative Solutions:** - Maybe there's a middle ground where the family can share responsibilities more fairly. The mom could contribute more, or the family could agree on a schedule that balances schoolwork and household duties. 6. **Cultural and Family Norms:** - Depending on cultural background, expectations around household chores and cooking can vary. It's possible that the mom has certain expectations based on her upbringing, but that doesn't necessarily make them fair or reasonable in this context. 7. **Long-term Effects:** - Constantly being the one to cook and manage the household can lead to resentment and burnout, especially for the student who is juggling school and family responsibilities. It's important for the family to recognize and address these issues to maintain a healthy home environment. 8. **Communication:** - Open and respectful communication is key. Instead of confrontational arguments, having a calm discussion about everyone's roles and responsibilities could lead to a more balanced and fair arrangement. In summary, while the student's frustration is understandable given the unfair distribution of responsibilities and the emotional toll of her mom's reactions, the way she handles the situation matters. Asserting her boundaries is important, but doing so respectfully and seeking a collaborative solution would be more constructive than refusing outright and causing further conflict.
